problem: Earlier vision-and-language navigation and grounding resources use simple visual input: object-centric photos, simulated worlds, or small indoor graphs. R2R, for example, has 90 houses averaging 119 panoramas and 6.0-panorama paths. Their language is fairly short and spatially shallow, and referring-expression datasets (4.4 to 8.5 tokens) only ask a model to tell objects of the same type apart, not to locate an arbitrary described point.
motivation: Real urban imagery changes both the vision problem and the kind of language people produce. It brings in many landmarks, reference to traffic flow, counting, conditional stopping ('until you see…') and allocentric relations between objects. A very large real street graph also rules out solving the task by search, so agents have to follow the instruction closely. A treasure-hunt collection setup, where writers are rewarded only if a follower actually finds the hidden bear, yields long but purposeful instructions that are validated by execution.
key_idea: Build a Google Street View navigation graph of NYC (29,641 panoramas) and collect 9,326 validated treasure-hunt instructions. Each one decomposes into (1) instruction-following navigation to a goal and (2) spatial description resolution (SDR), which means predicting the pixel where the hidden 'Touchdown' bear sits. SDR is posed as language-conditioned image reconstruction with LingUNet.
insight: The data demands much richer spatial reasoning than R2R. In 25 sampled dev examples, instructions mention 10.7 vs 3.7 unique entities per text, 21/25 contain temporal conditions (vs 7) and 21/25 require state verification (vs 2); navigation segments are mostly egocentric and SDR segments mostly allocentric. On SDR, fusing text as multi-scale 1x1 convolution kernels inside a UNet encoder-decoder (LingUNet, 32.83% dev acc@80px) clearly beats per-pixel concatenation (Concat 17.85, ConcatConv 18.00) and slightly beats a single text-generated 5x5 kernel (Text2Conv 29.36). A language-free UNet still reaches 10.86% acc@40px dev, which exposes visual priors in where workers hide the bear. For navigation, existing supervised models (RConcat, GA) reach only about 10% TC. The single-modality ablation shows they draw little on the text: removing text keeps most of the performance, while removing images kills learning. That ablation table appears to have its TC and SPD columns swapped. ResNet features beat raw RGB (dev TC 9.8 vs 6.8 for RConcat), and a pipeline of the best nav and SDR models finds Touchdown only 4.5% of the time, against about 92% for humans.
method: Street View environment: 29,641 NYC panoramas and 61,319 undirected edges, each attached to a heading. A state is (panorama, heading), and actions FORWARD/LEFT/RIGHT/STOP move along an edge or snap to the nearest edge heading to the left or right.

Four-stage crowdsourcing: (I) a writer follows a sampled 35-45-panorama route from a north-facing start, places Touchdown and writes instructions (no text or store names allowed); (II) the bear's location is propagated to neighbouring panoramas; (III) a follower validates by navigating without a map and clicking within 90px, with up to 5 clicks and 2 workers; (IV) tokens are segmented into navigation and SDR parts, which may overlap. Bonuses are tied to validation success.

Metrics: navigation uses TC (stop at the goal or a neighbouring node), SPD (graph shortest-path distance to the goal) and SED (success weighted by normalized Levenshtein distance between panorama sequences). SDR uses accuracy and consistency (all images of a sentence correct) at 40/80/120px radius, plus mean pixel distance.

LingUNet for SDR: a BiLSTM (300-d embeddings, 600 hidden) produces a mean-pooled text vector. The panorama is split into 8 perspective slices and encoded by an ImageNet ResNet (128x100x464 feature map). Two conv layers produce F1 and F2; each half of the text vector is linearly mapped to a 1x1x128x128 kernel that convolves F_k. Two deconvolutions with skip concatenation follow, then a per-pixel MLP and a softmax over pixels, trained with KL to a Gaussian-smoothed gold location. The prediction is the mode.

Navigation baselines: RConcat (Mirowski et al. 2018 adapted to instructions) concatenates an LSTM instruction encoding, a CNN over channel-averaged heading-centred ResNet features, and the previous action embedding into an LSTM, followed by a time-step embedding and softmax. GA uses gated attention of the instruction over CNN features.

Training: behaviour cloning (maximum likelihood on demonstration actions) with asynchronous Hogwild! plus Adam over 6 clients. Horizon is 55 in training and 50 at test, with early stopping on dev SPD. The full task is solved by pipelining the best nav model with LingUNet.

setting.backbone: Task-specific networks trained from scratch on frozen ImageNet-pretrained ResNet features: LingUNet (BiLSTM + conv/deconv) for SDR; RConcat / Gated-Attention (LSTM + CNN + LSTM policy) for navigation
setting.training_data: Touchdown train split only: 6,526 navigation examples and 17,880 SDR examples (7% of training held out for early stopping in SDR)
setting.observation: Navigation: perspective crop of the Street View panorama centred on the agent heading, as channel-averaged 100x100 ResNet features (or 84x84 RGB 60° view in an ablation) plus the instruction. SDR: full 360° RGB panorama as 8 perspective slices plus the description.
setting.action_space: discrete graph actions FORWARD (move along edge) / LEFT / RIGHT (turn to the nearest edge heading) / STOP; SDR outputs an (x,y) pixel
setting.simulator: Google Street View panorama graph of New York City (static released panoramas)

numbers_note:
This is a dataset paper. RConcat and GA are the authors' re-implementations of prior models, and LingUNet is adapted from Misra et al. 2018; they are listed as the paper's own experiments. SR = the paper's TC; SED is converted from fractions (e.g. 0.104 -> 10.4); SPD is kept as printed.

Results not included in the table:
- The full-task pipeline reaches 4.5% accuracy at 80px, but the split is not stated.
- Human performance is about 92%.
- In the single-modality ablation table ('Single-modality development results'), the TC and SPD columns appear swapped (e.g. RConcat NO-TEXT 'TC 24.48, SPD 7.26'), so it was left out.

The SDR example count is inconsistent: 27,575 in the intro vs 25,575 in the text and Table 2.
results: Touchdown navigation is very hard for supervised baselines. The best model, RConcat, reaches TC 10.7 / SPD 19.5 / SED 0.104 on test, above GA at 5.5 TC; Stop, Frequent and Random-walk baselines are at about 0-0.2 TC. On SDR, LingUNet is best: 34.59% test accuracy at 80px (consistency 14.57) and 708px mean error, beating Text2Conv (30.40), the language-free UNet and image-text concatenation baselines. A nav + SDR pipeline finds Touchdown only 4.5% of the time at 80px, against an estimated 92% for human workers.
limitations: The navigation models are only simple behaviour-cloned baselines that barely use language: the no-text ablation keeps most of the performance. The paper offers no method designed for the navigation task.
The environment is a static, NYC-only Street View graph without dynamics. Imagery is subject to Google's licensing, and panoramas must be re-downloaded, with some routes lost to Street View updates.

The navigation and SDR tasks are evaluated mostly separately; the full task is only a naive pipeline (4.5%). The dev/test splits come from the same city graph, so they do not test unseen-environment generalization.
builds_on: LingUNet (Misra et al. 2018; Blukis et al. 2018)
